procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The Food Inspector appealed the acquittal to the Bombay High Court. The High Court reversed the order of acquittal, convicting the appellant under Section 16(1)(a)(i) read with section 7 (i) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act and sentencing him to 6 months R.I. and a fine of Rs. 1,000.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave from the judgment and order of the Bombay High Court. The Supreme Court reduced the sentence to 3 months R.I. and a fine of Rs. 500, but dismissed the appeal in all other aspects.

issue.issue_text: Whether an accused can complain of being deprived of the right to have a food sample analysed by the Director under s. 13(2) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954, without having made an application for such analysis.

facts: A food inspector took a sample of buffalo milk from the appellant's shop, which was later found by a Public Analyst to be adulterated.
There was a long delay between when the sample was taken and when the prosecution commenced and the summons was served on the appellant.
The appellant was prosecuted under the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954.
The appellant argued that the delay deprived him of his right to have the sample analysed, as it would have decomposed, but he never actually filed an application to have it sent for analysis.
law: Section 13(2) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954, confers a right upon the accused to make an application to the court to have their part of the food sample sent to the Director of the Central Food Laboratory for analysis.
application: The Supreme Court determined that the right under s. 13(2) is not automatic; it must be actively invoked by the accused.
The Court held that for an accused to claim they have been deprived of this right, they must first make an application to the court as prescribed by the statute.

In this case, the appellant never applied to the court to have his sample analysed by the Director. He merely assumed, due to the delay, that the sample would be decomposed and that an application would be a "futile exercise."

The Court distinguished this situation from a prior case (Municipal Corporation of Delhi v. Ghisa Ram) where the accused had applied, but the Director reported the sample was too decomposed to be analysed. In that instance, the right was exercised but frustrated. Here, the right was never exercised at all.
The Court concluded that since the appellant failed to take the necessary step of filing an application, he could not complain that he was deprived of a right he never sought to use.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellant's complaint, holding that an accused cannot claim to be deprived of the right to have a food sample analysed by the Director under s. 13(2) of the Act if they have not first made an application to the court for such an analysis.

issue.issue_text: Whether a Magistrate can, without any evidence, conclude that a food sample has decomposed and is incapable of being analysed, thereby acquitting the accused.

facts: A food inspector took a sample of buffalo milk from the accused's shop.
The Public Analyst reported that the milk was adulterated as its fat content was below the prescribed limit.
The Magistrate acquitted the accused, reasoning that a long delay between taking the sample and serving the summons meant the sample must have decomposed.
The Magistrate concluded that this delay deprived the accused of their valuable right to have their portion of the sample independently analysed by the Director of the Central Food Laboratory.
The High Court reversed the acquittal, and the case was appealed to the Supreme Court.
law: Under Section 13(2) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954, an accused has a right to apply to the court to have their part of the food sample sent to the Director of the Central Food Laboratory for a second analysis.
application: The Supreme Court found that the Magistrate's conclusion that the sample had decomposed was based on speculation and assumption, not on any evidence presented in court.
The Court stated, "It was not for the Magistrate to decide without any data that the sample would be decomposed and was incapable of being analysed."

The Court emphasized that the accused never actually exercised their right under Section 13(2) by applying to have the sample sent for analysis. To claim that a right has been lost, one must first attempt to exercise it.
If the accused had applied, and the Director had then reported that the sample was decomposed and could not be analysed, only then could the accused argue that they were prejudiced by the delay.

The Court also noted that while a lower-than-prescribed amount of preservative (formalin) was used, the accused failed to provide any evidence to prove that this would have caused the sample to decompose and become unfit for analysis.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the Magistrate's reasoning, holding that a magistrate cannot acquit an accused by merely assuming, without any evidence, that a food sample has decomposed. The accused must first apply to have the sample analysed, and only if it is then found to be incapable of analysis can they claim that their right has been violated.

issue.issue_text: Whether the sentence of 6 months R.I. and a fine was appropriate in the facts and circumstances of the case.

facts: The appellant had entrusted the running of the shop to his nephew, the second accused.
There was no evidence that the shop had any mechanism to extract fat from the milk.
There was no evidence that water had been added to the milk.
law: The offence fell under proviso (1) of section 16 of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act.
Under this proviso, the Court was not bound to impose a mandatory sentence of 6 months imprisonment.
application: The Court determined that the original sentence of 6 months R.I. and a fine of Rs. 1,000 was not warranted in the circumstances of the case.
Considering the mitigating facts and the discretion allowed by the law, the Court decided to reduce the sentence.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court reduced the sentence from 6 months R.I. and a Rs. 1,000 fine to 3 months R.I. and a Rs. 500 fine, with a default sentence of one month R.I. for non-payment of the fine.

arguments.issue_text: Whether an accused can complain of being deprived of the right to have a food sample analysed by the Director under s. 13(2) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954, without having made an application for such analysis.
appellant_arguments: The appellant was deprived of his right to have the sample analysed by the Director due to the long delay in the service of summons by the prosecution.
This delay made it a futile exercise to send the sample for analysis, as it would have decomposed.
The loss of this valuable right, caused by the complainant's laches, entitled the appellant to an acquittal.
respondent_arguments: The appellant cannot complain of being deprived of a right he never sought to exercise.
To exercise the right under s. 13(2), the appellant was required to make an application to the court and pay the prescribed fee.
Since the appellant never filed an application, it cannot be said that he was deprived of any right.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a Magistrate can, without any evidence, conclude that a food sample has decomposed and is incapable of being analysed, thereby acquitting the accused.
appellant_arguments: The Magistrate was correct to conclude that the long delay between taking the sample and the start of the prosecution meant the sample must have decomposed.
This decomposition rendered the appellant's right to get his sample analysed meaningless.
respondent_arguments: It is not for the Magistrate to decide without any data or evidence that a sample has decomposed.
The Food Inspector had added a preservative (formalin) to the sample.
There was no evidence presented to the Magistrate that the sample had actually deteriorated or was incapable of being analysed.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the sentence of 6 months R.I. and a fine was appropriate in the facts and circumstances of the case.
appellant_arguments: The sentence was not called for in the circumstances of the case.
Mitigating factors existed: the appellant had entrusted the running of the shop to his nephew.
There was no evidence that fat had been deliberately extracted from the milk or that water had been added.
respondent_arguments: The sentence of 6 months R.I. and a fine of Rs. 1,000/- imposed by the High Court was appropriate for the conviction.

cases.case_name: Babulal Hargovindas v. The State of Gujarat
cases.principle: Unless an application to send the sample to the Director is made, the vendor cannot complain that he was deprived of his right to have the sample analysed by the Director.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A vendor cannot complain of being deprived of the right to have a sample analyzed by the Director of the Central Food Laboratory unless an application is made to send the sample to the Director.
obiter: It is not for a Magistrate to decide, without any data, that a sample would be decomposed and incapable of being analyzed.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: An accused cannot complain of being deprived of the valuable right to have a food sample analysed by the Director under s. 13(2) of the Act if they never made an application to exercise that right. A magistrate cannot acquit an accused by concluding, without any evidence, that a sample has decomposed and is incapable of analysis. While the conviction was therefore upheld, the sentence was reduced due to mitigating circumstances, including that the appellant had entrusted the shop to his nephew and there was no evidence of deliberate adulteration.
legal_tests_applied: The test for whether a conviction can be sustained when the right under s. 13(2) is at issue is whether 'the accused is prejudiced in his defence and is denied a valuable right of defending himself solely due to the daliberate acts of fhe prosecution'.
why_appellant_lost: The appellant never sought to exercise his right under s. 13(2), as he never applied to the court to have the part of the sample with him analysed by the Director.
The Magistrate's conclusion that the sample had decomposed was made without any data or evidence to justify it; it was not for the Magistrate to make such a determination.
No prejudice to the defence was actually shown, as it was not established on the record that the sample had deteriorated by the time the summons was received.

The appellant cannot complain of being deprived of a right he never sought to exercise, as the court held that 'unles' an applica-tion to send the sample to the Director is made, the vendor cannot complain that he was deprived of his right to have the sample analysed by the Director.'
why_respondent_won: The right under s. 13(2) is conditional; the appellant was required to make an application and pay the prescribed fee to have the sample sent to the Director, which he failed to do.

There was no evidence that the sample had decomposed. To the contrary, the Food Inspector had added a preservative (formalin) to the sample, and there was no evidence to suggest this was insufficient to preserve it for analysis.
The High Court's view to convict was in consonance with precedent, which establishes that a vendor cannot complain of being deprived of the right to analysis without first making an application.

There is no ·evidence to show that there was any mechanism in the shop by which the fat content could be extracted from un-'boiled milk.
